items.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
items.summary: The tech billionaire accuses Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using the network for military activity.
items.content:
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.

Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".

Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.

The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.

"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."

He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."

Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.

Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.

The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.

While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war .

Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.

Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.

The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.

Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.

Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.

Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.

It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.

Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

items.title: La fine del Sistema Solare potrebbe essere più rapida del previsto
items.summary: Anche i pianeti più esterni potrebbero non sopravvivere a lungo al Sole
items.content:
La fine del Sistema Solare potrebbe essere più rapida e caotica del previsto : si pensava che i pianeti più esterni, quindi Giove, Saturno, Urano e Nettuno, sarebbero sopravvissuti per miliardi di anni al Sole morente, ma una fine più violenta della nostra stella potrebbe cambiare drasticamente questo scenario. Lo indica lo studio pubblicato su The Astrophysical Journal Letters e guidato dal California Institute of Technology, che accorcia la possibile sopravvivenza di questi pianeti da cento miliardi a un solo miliardo di anni.

Si prevede che il Sole dovrebbe morire tra circa cinque miliardi di anni, quando esaurirà l'idrogeno presente nel suo nucleo. A quel punto, prima si espande , inghiottendo Mercurio e Venere . La Terra potrebbe venire risparmiata ma diventerebbe in ogni caso un mondo rovente e privo di vita . Dopo aver espulso gli strati esterni, il nucleo residuo del Sole si comprimerà , trasformandosi in una nana bianca destinata a raffreddarsi lentamente.

Per capire cosa succederà invece agli altri pianeti, i ricercatori guidati da Konstantin Batygin hanno combinato un modello dettagliato dell'evoluzione solare con programmi che tracciano le variazioni delle orbite di Giove, Saturno, Urano e Nettuno nei tre miliardi di anni dopo la morte della stella, testando 672 scenari differenti .

Se il Sole espellerà i suoi strati esterni con esplosioni violente, l'esito sarà quasi sicuramente nefasto: il 96% degli scenari mostra un'i nstabilità fatale entro tre miliardi di anni dalla trasformazione in nana bianca , e il 40% ottiene questo risultato ancora prima di tale evento . Alcune simulazioni, ad esempio, hanno portato all'espulsione di diversi pianeti dal Sistema Solare, mentre altri hanno visto Urano e Nettuno scambiarsi le orbite.

items.title: Funzionari iraniani al Nyt: 'Lecito colpire diplomatici americani'
items.summary: 'Israele e Usa hanno ucciso decine di funzionari e loro familiari'. Teheran avverte anche su Hormuz
items.content:
Due funzionari iraniani, uno dei quali membro dei Pasdaran, hanno detto al New York Times che l'ampliamento degli obiettivi di Teheran in caso di attacco include anche diplomatici e personale Usa. I funzionari, che hanno chiesto di rimanere anonimi, hanno confermato le notizie del Dipartimento di Stato relative al complotto iraniano volto a colpire cittadini americani.

I responsabili hanno difeso il piano: Israele e gli Stati Uniti "hanno ucciso decine di funzionari iraniani e alcuni loro familiari". A loro avviso, gli attacchi contro gli americani sono "leciti". Non è chiaro, tuttavia, se dispongano dei mezzi necessari per farlo.

Intanto da Teheran arriva un altro avvertimento: "Nulla tornerà allo stato in cui si trovava prima delle due recenti guerre, in particolare per quanto riguarda lo Stretto di Hormuz", afferma il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi, aggiungendo che "la guerra in corso ha cambiato tutto. Le rotte attraverso lo Stretto di Hormuz non saranno più quelle di un tempo".

Araghchi ha inoltre affermato che l'Iran ha sottolineato agli intermediari che la guerra deve cessare su tutti i fronti della regione, "altrimenti la pace rimarrà irraggiungibile".

Intanto Teheran ha attaccato con droni alcune postazioni curde anti-iraniane a Erbil, nel nord Iraq. Lo riferisce Fars. In precedenza erano state prese di mira basi del gruppo Komala nella regione del Balisan

items.title: 'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
items.summary: That Girl Boina's post about why she had closed her beauty parlour struck a nerve with other small business owners.
items.content:
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.

"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.

Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.

"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.

"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.

The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.

"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.

She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.

"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"

Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.

"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."

Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.

In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.

The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.

"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.

The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.

A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.

The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.

At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.

Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.

Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.

Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."

Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.

For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.

"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.

The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.

Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.

"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.

Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.

The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.

His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.

Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.

While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.

"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.

The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.

When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.

"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.

His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.

For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.

"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"

Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.

Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.

Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.

This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.

For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.

What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.

Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.

At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.

Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.

Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.

Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.

If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.

items.title: Midterm, Obama tira la volata a El-Sayed: 'C'è aria di cambiamento negli Usa'
items.summary: L'ex presidente Usa: 'Sento che in queste elezioni le persone sono pronte a qualcosa di nuovo'
items.content:
"Si respira aria di cambiamento". Così Barack Obama ha esordito sul palco di Detroit accanto al candidato democratico al senato in Michigan Abdul El-Sayed. Parlando dei quasi vent'anni trascorsi in politica, l'ex presidente ha scherzato dicendo di essere impegnato in campagne elettorali da troppo tempo. Poi ha aggiunto che proprio grazie a questa esperienza "riesco a capire quando arriva un'elezione che dà una sensazione un po' diversa".

"Un'elezione in cui le persone sono così pronte a qualcosa di nuovo, così desiderose di qualcosa di meglio, così stanche e sfinite da non poterne più, al punto che ovunque si vada si ha la sensazione che nell'aria ci sia un cambiamento. E in Michigan, è proprio questo che percepisco in questo momento", ha affermato Obama.

In un attacco neanche troppo velato a Donald Trump, Obama ha detto che a Washington c'è "bisogno di persone serie. Non è il momento per i reality show". Parlando a Detroit al comizio del candidato democratico al Senato in Michigan Abdul El-Sayed ha aggiunto che "dobbiamo assicurarci di eleggere candidati come lui". "Lui capisce ciò che ci affligge in questo momento, ciò che sta destabilizzando così tanto il Paese".

items.title: E' tornata l'ora solare, lancette indietro di un'ora
items.summary: Oltre ai minori consumi di energia con l'ora legale si sono ridotte le emissioni di CO2 per circa 140 mila tonnellate
items.content:
E' tornata l'ora solare nella notte tra sabato e domenica. Si chiude il periodo di ora legale che per quest'anno ha consentito minori consumi di energia e di ridurre le emissioni di CO2. Lo comunica Terna secondo i cui dati questo risultato ha portato a un risparmio economico di oltre 90 milioni di euro. I sette mesi di ora legale hanno prodotto benefici anche a livello ambientale, con una riduzione delle emissioni di CO2 stimata per circa 140 mila tonnellate, spiega Terna.

Secondo l'analisi di Terna, dal 2004 al 2026, il minor consumo di energia elettrica per l'Italia dovuto all'ora legale è stato complessivamente di oltre 12,3 miliardi di kWh e ha comportato, in termini economici, un risparmio per i cittadini di circa 2,4 miliardi di euro.

Il cambio dell'ora tra sabato 24 e domenica 25 ottobre: tra le 3 e le 2 lancette indietro di 60 minuti.

items.title: iPhone Duo, c'è un trucco per aprire il Centro di Controllo in modo più semplice
items.summary: Niente contorsionismi: così basta un tocco.
items.content:
Ora che iPhone Duo è uscito, e gli utenti ci hanno messo le mani sopra, cominciano ad emergere tutte quelle differenze nell'utilizzo quotidiano (di cui vi abbiamo parlato anche noi) e quelle criticità che prima non si potevano cogliere. Col suo formato inedito, il primo melafonino pieghevole ha spinto Apple a ripensare iOS, facendo scelte radicali come lo spostamento del dock nella parte destra del display.

BASTA UN TOCCO

Per i mancini iPhone Duo, essendo più largo di un iPhone tradizionale, non promette di essere molto comodo. items.title: Vaccino HPV: giù il rischio di parto prematuro
items.summary: Vaccino HPV: giù il rischio di parto prematuro
items.content:
Il vaccino contro il Papilloma virus umano (HPV), che sta facendo sperare nell'eradicazione dei tumori della cervice uterina e che riduce l'incidenza dei tumori testa-collo, potrebbe ridurre gli esiti avversi durante la gravidanza. In base a un ampio studio pubblicato sulla rivista medico-scientifica The BMJ, questo vaccino abbassa il rischio di parto pretermine e di altre complicanze per le gestanti, con gli effetti più marcati sulle donne che l'hanno ricevuto da più giovani.. Uno strumento di prevenzione potentissimo. È noto da tempo che un'infezione da HPV in gravidanza nonché i metodi utilizzati per trattare le lesioni causate dall'HPV possono aumentare il rischio di parto precoce. Ecco perché un filone di studi si sta concentrando sul vaccino contro l'HPV come potenziale strumento per difendere la salute delle donne e dei feti durante la gravidanza. Un gruppo di scienziati del Karolinska Institutet di Stoccolma, in Svezia, ha usato i registri nazionali sulla salute svedesi per vedere se un precedente vaccino contro l'HPV fosse associato a una riduzione del rischio di esiti avversi in gravidanza.. I ricercatori sono partiti dai dati relativi a 624.713 parti singoli, di donne al primo parto di età compresa tra i 16 e i 35 anni, avvenuti in Svezia tra il 2006 e il 2023. Il 15% delle pazienti avevano ricevuto il vaccino quadrivalente contro il Papillomavirus umano in precedenza, cioè un vaccino che protegge da quattro diversi ceppi di HPV (6, 11, 16 e 18).
Su questo materiale di partenza, gli scienziati hanno effettuato uno studio cosiddetto "caso-controllo": hanno confrontato i casi di donne che avevano avuto almeno un esito avverso durante la gravidanza con una serie di casi di donne usate come soggetti di controllo, della stessa e età e anno di concepimento, che non avevano avuto esiti avversi.
Le complicanze considerate sono state parto pretermine (prima della 37esima settimana); parto molto pretermine (dalle 28 alle 31 settimane), rottura prematura delle membrane (cioè la perdita di liquido amniotico prima dell'inizio del travaglio), parto di un neonato molto piccolo, morte di un feto prima o durante il parto o decesso del neonato.. Un vaccino che fa la differenza. Tenuto conto anche di altri fattori sanitari e non che avrebbero potuto influire sugli esiti avversi, il vaccino contro l'HPV è risultato associato a una minore probabilità di incorrere in tutti gli esiti avversi considerati. La protezione maggiore si è vista sulle donne vaccinate prima dei 17 anni (in Italia, il vaccino contro l'HPV è proposto e offerto gratuitamente a tutte le ragazze e i ragazzi che abbiano compiuto gli 11 anni).. Anche se i risultati sono solidi e il metodo affidabile, si tratta di uno studio osservazionale, che non può affermare che vi sia un nesso di causa-effetto tra il vaccino e gli esiti osservati. Tuttavia, affermano gli scienziati: «Insieme alle precedenti ricerche che dimostrano la sicurezza della vaccinazione contro il papillomavirus umano durante la gravidanza, i nostri risultati suggeriscono che la vaccinazione contro il papillomavirus umano non solo è sicura per quanto riguarda gli esiti della gravidanza, ma potrebbe anche conferire ulteriori benefici riducendo il rischio di eventi avversi»..

items.title: Mazda, da Hiroshima ad Aielli: un murale per raccontare la pace attraverso l'arte
items.summary: A Borgo Universo, in Abruzzo, l'artista Kotè firma un'opera ispirata a Sadako Sasaki. Un progetto di Mazda Italia che intreccia memoria storica, solidarietà e speranza in un...
items.content:
La memoria può trasformarsi in un messaggio per il futuro: è questo il significato del murale che Mazda Italia ha affidato all'artista Antonio Cotecchia, in arte Kotè, per Borgo Universo, ad Aielli, in Abruzzo. L'opera, ispirata alla storia di Sadako Sasaki, la bambina di Hiroshima diventata simbolo internazionale di pace e speranza, porta nello spazio pubblico una riflessione sul valore della vita, sulla solidarietà e sulla responsabilità individuale.Il progetto nasce dal legame profondo tra Mazda e Hiroshima, città in cui l'azienda affonda le proprie radici e dove, dopo il bombardamento atomico del 6 agosto 1945, gli stabilimenti contribuirono alle attività di soccorso e alla ripresa della comunità. Da questa storia prende forma un'iniziativa che mette in dialogo memoria e contemporaneità, affidando all'arte il compito di rendere un'esperienza del passato un'occasione di riflessione condivisa.

Sadako Sasaki, il simbolo di una speranza che attraversa le generazioni

Al centro del murale c'è la figura di Sadako Sasaki, sopravvissuta al bombardamento atomico di Hiroshima e divenuta, nel tempo, un simbolo universale di pace. La sua storia è legata alla tradizione giapponese dell'origami e alle gru di carta, associate alla perseveranza, alla speranza e al desiderio di un futuro migliore. Nell'interpretazione di Kotè, il volto della bambina si costruisce attraverso forme geometriche e campiture cromatiche che richiamano le pieghe della carta. Il ritratto e il profilo della gru si fondono così in una composizione dinamica, nella quale la memoria della tragedia incontra la possibilità di immaginare un domani diverso. L'opera va oltre la commemorazione storica: invita a interrogarsi sul rapporto con gli altri e sul valore dei gesti quotidiani. La pace, in questa prospettiva, non è soltanto un principio astratto, ma una responsabilità che si traduce nella capacità di riconoscere il dolore altrui e di agire concretamente per gli altri.[gallery ids="292407,292408,292409,292411"]

Hiroshima, una storia di solidarietà e ricostruzione

Il legame tra Mazda e Hiroshima racconta una storia di resilienza che attraversa oltre un secolo. Fondata nel 1920 come Toyo Cork Kogyo, l'azienda ha condiviso l'evoluzione industriale e sociale della città, affrontando anche le conseguenze della tragedia del 1945.Gli stabilimenti, situati a circa cinque chilometri dall'ipocentro, subirono danni relativamente limitati rispetto ad altre aree urbane. Gli edifici rimasti utilizzabili furono messi a disposizione della comunità e impiegati per accogliere i feriti e sostenere i soccorsi. Alcuni spazi ospitarono temporaneamente anche uffici e organismi pubblici. Le testimonianze di chi visse quei giorni restituiscono il valore umano di questa esperienza. Tra loro, le giovani lavoratrici Mieko Sakamoto, Tomiko Kuwata e Toshie Nishikawa, che prestarono aiuto ai feriti in condizioni estreme, con risorse insufficienti e senza una preparazione medica specifica.Parallelamente, l'azienda avviò il percorso di ripresa produttiva. Nel dicembre 1945, a pochi mesi dal bombardamento, riprese la produzione dei camion a tre ruote, destinati a contribuire alla ricostruzione della città e al ritorno alla vita quotidiana. Una storia nella quale il lavoro e l'innovazione si intrecciano con la solidarietà, mostrando come la capacità di ripartire possa assumere un significato che va oltre la dimensione industriale.[gallery ids="292403,292401,292404,292402"]

Dall'innovazione all'arte, il valore delle persone

La storia di Mazda è segnata anche dalla ricerca di soluzioni originali e dalla volontà di affrontare sfide tecniche complesse. Dal Mazda-Go, il primo veicolo del marchio presentato nel 1931, allo sviluppo del motore rotativo, fino alla filosofia di design Kodo - Soul of Motion e al lavoro dei Takumi, gli artigiani che mettono esperienza e attenzione al dettaglio al servizio delle vetture, l'innovazione si è accompagnata a una costante attenzione alla qualità e alla sensibilità progettuale.Il murale di Aielli si inserisce in questo percorso come un'espressione diversa della stessa attenzione alla dimensione umana. Attraverso il linguaggio dell'arte urbana, Mazda condivide una parte della propria storia e la trasforma in un messaggio accessibile, capace di raggiungere persone e generazioni differenti.

Aielli, un luogo d'incontro tra memoria e contemporaneità

La scelta di Borgo Universo non è casuale. Ad Aielli, l'arte contemporanea è diventata parte integrante del paesaggio e della vita della comunità, trasformando le superfici degli edifici in occasioni d'incontro tra creatività, territorio e partecipazione. In questo contesto, il murale di Kotè porta una storia nata a Hiroshima in uno spazio condiviso, dove residenti, visitatori e nuove generazioni possono incontrarla e reinterpretarla. Mazda Italia riafferma così il valore di una visione che mette al centro le persone. Dalla ricostruzione di Hiroshima all'arte di Aielli, il filo conduttore è la possibilità di trasformare le difficoltà in occasioni di crescita, senza dimenticare il passato. Perché costruire un futuro migliore significa anche riconoscere il valore di ogni vita e tradurre la speranza in azioni concrete: un percorso nel quale il "Joy of Driving" si apre a una visione più ampia, quella del "Joy of Living".

items.title: Sicurezza: la NHTSA propone luci ciano per le auto a guida autonoma
items.summary: La nuova proposta di aggiornamento della norma FMVSS n. 108 introduce indicatori turchese opzionali per i veicoli senza conducente come il Cybercab.
items.content:
La National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) ha presentato una proposta di regolamentazione per riformare la norma di sicurezza federale FMVSS n. 108 sull'illuminazione dei veicoli a motore. La riforma è concepita specificamente per accogliere i veicoli a guida autonoma (ADS) privi di volante, pedali e specchietti tradizionali, come il Cybercab di Tesla. Il tema è di grande attualità, soprattutto dopo l'apertura di un'inchiesta sul servizio robotaxi di Tesla proprio a causa della mancanza di comandi fisici, la cui risposta ufficiale è attesa entro il 30 ottobre.

Luci ciano per i veicoli che viaggiano in modalità autonoma

La novità principale della proposta riguarda l'introduzione opzionale delle luci di segnalazione ADS di colore ciano (turchese), standardizzate secondo le specifiche SAE J578 e SAE J3134. Queste lampade indicano chiaramente che il veicolo sta viaggiando in modalità di guida totalmente autonoma, ossia senza che sia richiesta l'attenzione o la supervisione attiva di un occupante umano a bordo. Per questo motivo, le luci ciano saranno riservate ai sistemi senza conducente e vietate sui veicoli con guida assistita che richiede il monitoraggio umano, come Tesla FSD (Supervised).

Non sarà un obbligo di legge

I costruttori potranno installare da una a due luci ciano sulla parte anteriore, sui lati e sul retro (da quattro a otto lampade totali) ad un'altezza minima di 15 pollici (circa 38 cm) dal suolo. Le luci dovranno rimanere fisse ed attivarsi in modo sincrono. L'adozione rimarrà facoltativa: l'agenzia intende standardizzare il segnale visivo senza imporlo ai produttori, richiamando un sondaggio su oltre 4.400 conducenti e i test condotti da Mercedes-Benz con Drive Pilot in California.

Eliminati alcuni comandi fisici

Oltre all'illuminazione ciano, la proposta abolisce importanti vincoli strutturali per le autovetture prive di comandi manuali. Per i veicoli senza volante o pedali non saranno più richiesti i comandi fisici azionati a mano o a pedale per indicatori di direzione, luci d'emergenza e abbaglianti, né le relative spie sul cruscotto. Il sistema informatico dell'auto gestirà le luci via software, dovendo integrare soltanto una spia di guasto visibile da ogni sedile. La riforma aggiorna inoltre i test dei fari a fascio integrale alla tensione dichiarata dal costruttore anziché a 12,8 V.La bozza, in consultazione pubblica per 30 giorni sul Federal Register, traccia una cornice regolatoria più definita per i robotaxi. Nei prossimi mesi vedremo come evolverà il quadro normativo negli Stati uniti per le auto a guida autonoma.

items.title: Eni proroga il price cap sui carburanti fino al 31 dicembre 2026
items.summary: Confermato il tetto a 1,99 euro per la benzina e 2,25 euro per il diesel, il gruppo rivendica la responsabilità sociale d'impresa mentre i consumatori sollecitano il Governo.
items.content:
A seguito del prolungarsi delle tensioni geopolitiche e delle criticità sul mercato degli idrocarburi, Eni ha annunciato la proroga del calmiere sui prezzi di benzina e gasolio fino al 31 dicembre 2026. La misura, introdotta a fine settembre sulla rete Enilive, fissa il tetto massimo a 1,99 euro al litro per la benzina e a 2,25 euro al litro per il diesel. L'annuncio della conferma del "price cap" è giunto dall'amministratore delegato Claudio Descalzi durante la presentazione dei conti del terzo trimestre, caratterizzati da utile netto in crescita e aumento del buyback.

L'introduzione della misura e le condizioni di mercato

La decisione di calmierare i listini affonda le sue radici nei complessi scenari del 2026. Il 25 settembre il gruppo ha comunicato l'avvio del price cap dal 28 settembre, con un risparmio stimato in 7 centesimi rispetto alla media alla pompa. La scelta è stata motivata con la contrazione dell'offerta dovuta alle crisi geopolitiche ed alla ridotta capacità di raffinazione europea. L'iniziativa ha spinto anche le altre maggiori compagnie ad intervenire, ma Eni si è distinta per la chiarezza nell'indicare i massimali.

Le dichiarazioni dell'ad Descalzi

Sulla flessibilità del tetto fissato per i prossimi mesi, l'amministratore delegato Claudio Descalzi ha spiegato:
Confermiamo che ne valuteremo il valore ma manterremo il concetto di price cap fino a fine anno. Per quanto riguarda il suo livello, attualmente a 2,25 euro per il gasolio e 1,99 euro per la benzina, monitoreremo le dinamiche di mercato e prezzo, nonché le forniture effettivamente disponibili in rapporto alla nostra struttura logistica per valutarlo nel corso del periodo.
Descalzi ha ricordato che il prezzo alla pompa dipende da molteplici variabili oltre al barile. Inoltre, l'amministratore delegato ha evidenziato la risposta degli automobilisti:
Abbiamo avuto più di 900 stazioni di servizi con scorte esaurite perché non avevano più prodotti, anche se le rifornivamo due volte al giorno.

La responsabilità sociale

Parlando con gli analisti, Francesco Gattei, Chief Transition & Financial Officer di Eni, ha illustrato il valore etico ed economico dell'operazione:
Per noi fare impresa significa gestire una strategia volta a perseguire un valore sostenibile e a lungo termine. Crediamo che le aziende abbiano una responsabilità sociale, non possiamo vivere in una sorta di bolla al di fuori del mondo reale. Quindi vogliamo e dobbiamo essere realistici e pensare che sostenere i clienti sia una priorità per un'azienda che si occupa di un bisogno fondamentale com'è l'energia. Per questo abbiamo deciso di introdurre un tetto massimo alle nostre vendite di benzina e diesel.
In merito all'impatto economico, Gattei ha precisato che:
Il tetto verrà rivalutato periodicamente. In termini di stime, riteniamo che, nelle attuali condizioni di mercato e ipotizzando il livello osservato finora, l'impatto in un trimestre si attesterà nell'ordine di alcune centinaia di milioni.

Le reazioni delle associazioni dei consumatori

La decisione di estendere il tetto è stata accolta favorevolmente dai consumatori. Massimiliano Dona, presidente dell'Unione Nazionale Consumatori, ha dichiarato:
Bene che Eni prosegua con il price cap fino a fine anno, ma non deve diventare un alibi per il Governo per lavarsene le mani come Ponzio Pilato, tradendo persino gli impegni, già inadeguati, presi sul meccanismo delle accise mobili il 16 settembre in conferenza stampa, altrimenti l'impegno di Eni finisce per essere oscurato da risvolti negativi e dall'irresponsabilità del Governo.

items.title: Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
items.summary: Ukraine needs another satellite internet service, but a decent alternative to Elon Musk's network doesn't exist - yet.
items.content:
Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.

That vulnerability was highlighted by Musk himself on Saturday, when he accused Ukraine of violating Starlink's terms of service by using it for "drone strikes to kill people".

Saying that loophole was closed last week, he wrote on X , external : "Violation of those terms will result in end of service."

He added: "Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately".

There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.

France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared with Starlink's 10,000-plus.

The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, Iris², however it won't be up and running until 2029.

For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.

"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."

For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.

Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield, which is controlled by the US government, for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.

"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.

Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored , highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.

"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.

Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Musk.

While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.

"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."

Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to agree.

Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield", a soldier said.

The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.

Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones", said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.

Rhetoric from the White House - like Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.

She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.

Comments from Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted , external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.

Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently", a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.

Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.

But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.

That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.

Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing because, as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.

Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".

No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.

But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."

Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, Iris² , external is up and running in 2029.

The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared ) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.

Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.

It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.

"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that Iris² is planning for less satellites."

Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".

A highly produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With Iris², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."

So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.

"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."

It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."

But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."

Iris² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE , external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.

And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.

Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need " a lot of money".

Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.

"Even if you gave me €8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.

Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.

"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."

items.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
items.summary: The Israeli Defense Forces announces restrictions on the movement of Palestinian workers in the run-up to Tuesday's election.
items.content:
All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.

The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.

The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.

It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.

Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced .

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which has led to at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened, according to footage shared online.

Even before the entry and exit bans on workers were announced by the IDF on Sunday, the military had cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.

It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.

Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, just days ahead of Israel's election taking place on Tuesday.

In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, Netanyahu threatened a "very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.

Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was being "driven by the elections" and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far right and the settlers.

On Saturday, thousands gathered in Tel Aviv for a large anti-government demonstration.

The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by militants on 7 October 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack.

"Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.

The gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu.

items.title: Marina Abramović’s “love letter” to Rome: a gilded bronze donkey
items.summary: Ahead of her 80th birthday, the artist opens up about inspiration, creativity, and her deepest fears. In the Italian capital she unveils a sculpture born out of a dialogue with Alda Fendi
items.content:
The first surprise when you come face to face with Marina Abramović is her long, lingering smiles, one after another. The gaze of the woman who stripped the art audience of its innocence is every bit as stern as the chronicles say, but it is also ironic and amused.

Perhaps it has something to do with the oversized red glasses framing a face impervious to tears—and, as it seems, to time itself. The sense of intimidation the artist inspires via Zoom falls just short of what her world-renowned performances evoke, leaving audiences stunned into absolute silence.

The distance of the screen helps. And above all, this time, we are allowed to ask questions. Starting with one about a little donkey.

We see it stepping forward beside Abramović, who looks straight ahead with the proud, impenetrable expression that has become her trademark. In the background lies the Roman Forum.

No gun, no blade: none of the seventy-two objects that, in 1974 during Rhythm 0 in Naples, the artist placed at the disposal of spectators, authorizing them to do whatever they wished with her body.

This time, she is accompanied by a gentle, patient creature featured in a gilded bronze sculpture—the first Abramović has ever created in this medium.

A “love letter to Rome,” as she defines it herself, as she prepares to turn eighty on November 30. The work, commissioned by the Alda Fendi Foundation-Experiments, will be installed beneath the newly restored Arch of Janus.

We are standing near the Church of Santi Luca e Martina, a Baroque masterpiece by Pietro da Cortona. Outside the windows lies a breathtaking view of the Roman Forum. Inside, the screen displays images of Abramović connecting from New York.

Beside us is Alda Fendi, our host and president of the foundation that bears her name, and an arts patron known for bringing contemporary art and historic heritage together.

The two women speak to each other with the enthusiasm of people who met too late and now want to make up for lost time. The connection glitches more than once. “There’s too much energy circulating between us,” the artist says.

Ms. Abramović, what are you doing in Rome beside a little donkey, looking like a shepherdess or a pilgrim? Does this have anything to do with the months you spent making pecorino cheese in Sardinia back in the 1970s?

“With Ulay—my long-time partner in life and art—I lived in a van for years, traveling with no set destination. In Orgosolo, we stayed for three months. We lived with the shepherds and looked after a flock of a hundred sheep. I learned to milk them and turn milk into cheese. We ate carasau bread; I knitted.

I was fascinated by the traditions of that land, its ancient rituals. Even by the reputation of the bandits: when I asked where they were, the locals replied that they were the bandits. I had very little, but I was free. Those were among the happiest years of my life.”

“No. I was unhappy, very much so. I grew up in a family that belonged to the Yugoslav establishment. My mother was a national heroine; my father was a general. We lived in a kind of red bourgeoisie, all piano lessons and military discipline. It was a controlled existence.

My mother was extremely strict. Up until I was twenty-nine years old, I had to be home by ten at night. I was already an artist, doing performances, exploring the boundaries of freedom, and yet I had to be home by ten.

My grandmother, on the other hand, was deeply religious. She was the one who passed on a sense of spirituality to me. As a child, that dimension allowed me to escape reality. Then I ran away for real. I left home and never went back. I didn't see my mother again until ten years later.”

Did your need to fight for your freedom stem from that childhood?

“That, and the need to prove something. People used to tell me that everything was easy for me, that I was the daughter of important people, that I held a privileged position. I wanted to prove that I could make it on my own. I was very proud of my choice.

Today, I can say that I made it. And above all, I am much happier now than I was in my thirties or forties.”

In 1974, in Naples, for Rhythm 0 , you stood motionless for six hours, allowing the public to do whatever they wanted to your body. Someone cut your clothes, others injured you, and others even pointed a gun at you. Would you ever put an audience in a position to hurt you again?

“Absolutely not. I learned my lesson. In Naples, I realized that if you give people the chance to do anything, they can go so far as to kill you.

Today, my relationship with the audience is completely different. They cannot touch me; they cannot speak to me. I have no need to repeat that experience. I already know what can happen.”

With The Artist Is Present at MoMA in New York in 2010, you spent more than seven hundred hours sitting across from strangers. You are a living archive of humanity. What did you learn?

“That there are no bad people. It is the circumstances, the realities in which we live, that can make us wicked. In people's eyes, I saw suffering, loneliness, melancholy. But also an immense amount of love. I looked 1,565 people in the eye. And I remember those gazes, one by one.

The surprising thing is that, after a while, they were no longer looking at me: they began looking inside themselves. I was merely a mirror. I saw their fragilities, their pains, the emotions we normally hide coming to the surface. Some remained seated for hours, completely losing all sense of time.

And I ended up knowing strangers more intimately than I had ever known members of my own family. It is extraordinary what can happen between two human beings without pronouncing a single word.”

“People wait for hours before they can sit in front of me. And when their turn comes, they are observed by others and by me; they are photographed. They can do nothing; they have nowhere to hide. They must sit there, alone with themselves.

And so they begin to cry. Because suddenly they meet their own feelings and their own loneliness. Some people return. They sleep outside the museum to repeat the experience. It is extraordinary how many things can happen without speaking a single word. The eyes are the soul.”

Alda Fendi: “That is what I love about your art, Marina. You give people the chance to recognize something of themselves. That is the essence of the work we are preparing for Rome. An extraordinary opportunity you are offering to this city.”

Marina Abramović: “It is a confession of the soul. A chance to open oneself up. To me, this work is a love letter to Rome. I want it to contain something people can feel intimately, something that belongs to their lives.”

Alda Fendi explains that the little donkey is no coincidence. As part of the Foundation’s artistic research, the animal has already featured prominently in a series of works exploring spirituality and fragility, inspired by Prayer to Go to Paradise with the Donkeys by French poet Francis Jammes.

A stubborn and gentle creature, burdened for centuries with the weight of humanity, now accompanies a woman famed for turning her own body into a battlefield. Beneath a 4th-century Roman arch, the gilded bronze promises a striking contrast between monumentality and tenderness.

Ms. Abramović, in a world that is dematerializing, do you feel the body is losing its centrality?

“The body is everything. The body is the universe. The body is what we have to know the world and ourselves. But a single lifetime is not enough to fully understand it. You must know the mind, the spirit, your fears, your limits. I have used my body all my life precisely to try to understand how far I could go. And, above all, to free myself from fear.

Naturally, the body ages. And as it ages, it reveals new limitations, reminding you that life is finite. But it continues to teach you something.”

“In nature. I need to be alone, to walk along a river, to hug trees. I need places where you can still feel an ancient wisdom. I have learned a vast amount from Aborigines and shamans. I love monasteries.”

In 1988, you and Ulay set off from opposite ends of the Great Wall of China to meet each other after nearly three months of walking. It was meant to be a celebration of your love, but the interminable delays in obtaining Chinese permits turned it into the most famous farewell in art history. What did you learn from that journey?

“I was always walking in front of everyone. I wanted to be first, as had always happened to me in life. And I didn't understand why the guides kept staying behind me. At one point, I asked why. They answered with a proverb: the most fragile birds fly first . It struck me deeply.

I had always thought that being in front meant being strong, brave, leading others. Instead, according to that ancient wisdom, it could mean the exact opposite. So I changed my position and started walking behind. I learned that it is not necessary to always be first.”

When a love story like the one between you and Ulay becomes a work of art and then the love ends, who gets to keep the artwork?

items.title: Seeing the world through sound: Hildegard of Bingen at the Vatican’s Venice Biennale pavilion
items.summary: The 12th-century Benedictine abbess, mystic and visionary inspires a journey through music, poetry and silence in the Lagoon City
items.content:
Some visitors leave in tears. Others feel the need to embrace. Still others remain silent for a long time.

It is not sadness. But you cannot quite call it happiness either. It is something else: the feeling of returning from somewhere beyond.

Spread across two venues — the Discalced Carmelite Garden in Cannaregio and Santa Maria Ausiliatrice in Castello — the Holy See Pavilion is a “pilgrim” pavilion, as Cardinal José Tolentino de Mendonça describes it.

Prefect of the Dicastery for Culture and Education and commissioner of the pavilion, he has overseen one of the most surprising and moving contributions to the Venice Biennale, perhaps the most remarkable of all.

Curated by Hans Ulrich Obrist and Ben Vickers, together with Soundwalk Collective, the pavilion is dedicated to Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), the 12th-century German Benedictine abbess, healer, mystic and visionary.

It also takes its title from her: The ear is the eye of the soul.

We meet Cardinal Tolentino de Mendonça in his Vatican offices to take stock of the pavilion's reception now that the Biennale has passed its halfway point. But first, what exactly is there to see and hear?

At Santa Maria Ausiliatrice, visitors encounter the final work of Alexander Kluge, the artist, filmmaker and writer who died on 25 March before he could complete it.

The work brings together 12 stations in a journey through time — visual, musical and philosophical — beginning in a 12th-century convent, among Hildegard's contemporaries Abelard, Averroes and Maimonides, and the fantastic creatures of medieval bestiaries.

From there, it moves towards Gershom Scholem's interpretation of the Zohar, the foundational text of Jewish mysticism, and a tribute to Luigi Nono, bearing the beautiful title The Ear Bathes in the Holy Lake.

At the other end of Venice, in the Mystical Garden in Cannaregio, poetic and musical installations by artists from across the world — Brian Eno, Jim Jarmusch, Caterina Barbieri, Meredith Monk, Bhanu Kapil, Laraaji, Raúl Zurita and Kazu Makino — dissolve into one another as visitors wander through the garden, listening.

It is unexpected. What is striking about the Holy See's contribution to the Biennale is that its approach to contemporary art is not overtly confessional. That is the first cliché to be dismantled.

“The Church's presence in the cultural sphere is about connecting with a shared heritage, not simply promoting its own religious traditions,” Cardinal Tolentino de Mendonça explains.

“The pavilion resonates because it is universal. We can always identify a shared spiritual thirst, a question, a search, among the Magnifica Humanitas to which Pope Leo XIV dedicated his encyclical.

“Question by question, we can enter into dialogue. Art moves like a metaphor, a parable, an opening up another dimension of time. It is a privileged space for listening to one another. We invited genuine artists, believers and non-believers alike.”

The same principle, he adds, will guide the Dicastery's new initiative, the Contemporary Art Triennial of Catholic Universities, entitled Exercises in Empathy.

It has already opened in Rio de Janeiro and Santiago, Chile, and will expand to Bogotá, Boston, Milan, Lisbon and Luanda.

In the Mystical Garden, Caterina Barbieri's electronic music resonates beside a flowerbed of sage and daisies. The Twelve Questions of Anglo-Indian poet Bhanu Kapil can be heard beneath an elm tree, while Patti Smith's verses emerge from beneath rose bushes.

Hildegard's compositions drift along a row of vines. In the words of Meredith Monk, “Dancing voice, singing body”: here, the voice dances and the body sings.

The garden brings to life the vision Hildegard expressed in her work Scivias through the concept of viriditas.

“A word that is the bane of translators,” the cardinal says with a smile.

“It evokes so many things: the life force of greenery, fertility, healing power. I would call it a spiritual breath. I would also call it empathy.

“The Earth needs the spirit of spring, strength and hope. To speak of viriditas is to remind ourselves that creation always carries life-giving sap within it, and that this sap continues to flow through us, even in these parched times.”

That all this became a contemplative journey through sound was the result, if not of chance, then of a shared fascination.

“At an art biennale, you expect an overwhelmingly visual experience. But the visual arts have an unbreakable relationship with the invisible. Images teach us to perceive what cannot be seen; sound teaches us silence.

“Hans Ulrich Obrist's one condition was that we should focus on Hildegard. We visited several places. The Holy See does not have a permanent national pavilion. We are pilgrims.

“Obrist has retained an extraordinary capacity for wonder. You might expect someone who makes a living out of being amazed to lose that ability, wouldn't you? But he still possesses it.

“When we entered the Discalced Carmelite Garden, his words were: ‘This is magical.’

“In a garden, every moment is new. To inhabit it requires sensitivity and intelligence. Listening to Soundwalk Collective, I felt as though I could hear a blade of grass singing.”

Yet it is impossible — and would be wrong — to forget that beyond the walls of this hortus conclusus, this enclosed garden, 56 armed conflicts are raging.

“That is true. We live in a broken, wounded world, where human life is trampled upon.

“In his great work at Santa Maria Ausiliatrice, Alexander Kluge writes: ‘We live in a time of catastrophe. But that helps us better understand our need for consolation.’

“Stories console us. In searching for Hildegard's face, Kluge, like a modern-day Scheherazade and one of the world's last great storytellers, composes his own song, a final testament.

“This is a dark hour. But as Cristina Campo used to say, it is precisely when the soul falters that we must look to the lilies of the field.

“What can save us is rediscovering the garden. A garden is the womb of the world.”

items.title: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria
items.summary: Police are searching for other casualties, with officials warning the actual death toll could rise further.
items.content:
Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police say.

There are fears the actual death toll is much higher, with eyewitnesses speaking of 20 lives lost and a non-governmental organisation suggesting a toll of as many as 50.

The gunmen reportedly swooped on the village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area mounted on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers on Friday in a rampage that went on for up to four hours.

Police say they are searching for other casualties in the bush but the authorities were accused by Amnesty International of failing to protect rural communities.

Nigeria continues to face attacks by armed groups across several regions, including the northwest, northeast and central regions.

The country is also battling a jihadist insurgency in its north-east that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of insecurity.

Following the latest incident, police said they recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call.

The attackers had fled by the time they arrived but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, they told BBC News on Saturday.

"We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen though there was no casualty on their side and ours because the terrain is difficult and they're used to the terrain," Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said.

He added that officers were continuing to search the bush nearby for people who might have been killed or wounded, and warned the death toll could still rise.

Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece.

"They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions," he said. "They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack."

The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria

'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis

Survivors who spoke to AFP said they had counted at least 20 dead.

"People were running in different directions to escape the attack," Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said. "Nobody knew where it was safe to go."

Another survivor, Sa'idu Nuhu, said that some people were still missing.

Amnesty's Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, told BBC News on Saturday that the NGO had spoken to some of the bereaved families who said up to 50 people had died.

Sanusi called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities "at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity".

items.title: Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections
items.summary: Obama said the election was "the last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration".
items.content:
Former US President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections.

"This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America".

The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.

Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.

Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members while speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House.

"After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough'," the former president said in Cleveland.

Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy.

"If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".

Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down".

The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs" and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.

He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders".

Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested".

Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'"

In Ohio, the current president faced an attack from his predecessor over the war in Iran, with Obama telling Democrat supporters the conflict had given Tehran "veto power" over the Strait of Hormuz.

When asked about the war earlier in the day, Trump said: "I've done it very effectively and I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win."

He was also asked whether Melania Trump would would visit Ukraine after the White House announced she secured a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city. "We will see," he said.

At his afternoon rally, Obama also took a swipe at Trump's efforts to renovate the White House.

"What's with all the gold? He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory," Obama joked.

Obama's rally in Ohio was to show support for ex-Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running to unseat incumbent Republican Senator John Husted, and Amy Acton, who is running for state governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

Obama criticised Ramaswamy for a campaign ad released last week in which Acton's estranged mother was featured calling her a liar. The ad didn't mention that the woman's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross. No low he will not sink to try to get in the limelight," Obama said. "I mean, think about this latest ad he ran."

Acton also spoke at the campaign rally before Obama to argue that Ramaswamy "has chosen to exploit my childhood" to "save his struggling campaign".

'This is despicable': Amy Acton responds to Ohio attack ad featuring her estranged mother

One of the most frequently asked questions we get is how we deploy large models on Cerebras wafer-scale chips. A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.

In this post, we’ll explain how we split a large frontier model across multiple WSE-3T wafers, to run multi-trillion parameter models at 1000-2000+ tokens per second.

We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.

Kimi K3 is an open source, 3T parameter model with 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers.

It scores an impressive 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 88.8%) and 91.2% on BrowseComp (vs. GPT-5.6 Sol's 90.4%). These results demonstrate frontier-level coding and agentic capabilities, even outperforming leading proprietary models on some benchmarks. Read more about Kimi K3 here .

To calculate the total number of Cerebras WSE-3T wafers we need to support Kimi K3, let’s first calculate the size of each model layer.

Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is:

Now that we know each layer needs about 16 GB, we can figure out how many layers fit on each 44 GB wafer. The answer depends on the layer type:

Therefore, with Kimi K3’s 69 linear layers and 24 dense layers , we get:

Cerebras executes models in a pipeline. After the Cerebras compiler maps the model layers across regions of wafers, the runtime maps the path for tokens to flow between wafers. For ultrafast latency, only activations need to be passed between the wafers, and this can be done via RDMA over Ethernet. This is roughly 2 microseconds per hop.

It’s important to emphasize that because each Cerebras wafer has 44 GB of on-chip SRAM and each layer is only 16 GB, we are typically able to fit entire layers of the model directly on the chip.

This means that in most cases, the model weights never have to move, and layers don’t need to be split across wafers. Only activations cross from one wafer to the next.

Now that we have our wafers connected together and the model laid out, we can think of each wafer as one stage in an assembly line: the model’s weights for each stage stay in place, and the request’s intermediate results move through the layer stages.

For example, Wafer 1 runs model layers 1–2 and sends its activations to wafer 2. Wafer 2 runs layers 3–4 and passes its results to Wafer 3, and so on until the last wafer produces the next token.

This raises a common misconception. If a token has to travel through each wafer in order, doesn’t each wafer sit idle while it waits for its turn? In effect, wouldn't the system be running at a batch size of one?

No! If we only sent one request down the line at a time and waited for it to complete before starting the next request, this would be an inefficient use of the pipeline. Instead, we keep the entire pipeline full with different requests. Because the model is split into pipeline stages already, each stage can work on a different request at the same time.

While stage 3 processes a token for request A, stage 2 processes one for request B, and stage 1 one for request C. In our example, each stage is a layer. In production, Cerebras uses much finer-grained stages, and many more of them.

Each stage can also process a micro-batch , a small group of requests, rather than a single request. So the number of requests in flight is roughly the number of stages times the micro-batch size.

To understand the tradeoff, smaller micro-batches make each request even faster, while larger micro-batches increase total throughput.

The amount of on-chip memory allocated to KV cache determines the maximum number of concurrent requests. Every request in flight needs its own KV cache on each dense-layer wafer, so the size of on-chip memory sets the ceiling on concurrent requests. As explained above, we only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.

For each 44 GB wafer that already has one dense layer, we can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with:

Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer. In this case:

To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up:

To then calculate the total number of concurrent requests this configuration would support, we divide:

The total number of concurrent requests represents the number of simultaneous requests moving through the pipeline at any point in time. Unlike a GPU batch, those requests don’t wait for one another to finish, they stream through the pipeline continuously.

Of course, neither concurrency nor batch size tells you exactly how efficiently an inference system performs. When evaluating the throughput of an inference system, the more meaningful metric is total token throughput per unit of power (e.g. tokens per second per megawatt), when measured at the same output generation speed.

The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.
